segments.heading: The denoiser's tensor-core parity
lines: Case study: the denoiser's tensor-core parity.
Last lesson measured where 16-bit numbers run out. Tonight Rerun follows a real case where they did: a check that failed, the search for why, and the fix that was not made.

segments.heading: Two paths, one check
lines: raw-native is a renderer with a small neural denoiser. Its network runs two ways on the graphics chip: one on the tensor cores, with 16-bit inputs and weights and 32-bit sums, and one in plain 32-bit arithmetic.
Before either ships, a parity check compares every output value with a reference. The rule is fixed in advance: no value may differ by more than {{recipe.bound}}.

On an RTX 4090, over {{primary.rtx.frames|int}} frames, the 32-bit path's worst difference was {{primary.rtx.scalar.max_abs|f4}}. The tensor-core path's was {{primary.rtx.coop.max_abs|f4}}, at frame {{primary.rtx.coop.max_at_frame}}.

predict.question: The tensor-core path missed by ten times the bound. Wrong everywhere, or in a few places?

segments.heading: A few places
lines: In a few places. Out of {{primary.rtx.coop.values|int}} values, the average difference was about six millionths, and 99.99 percent were under {{primary.rtx.coop.p99_99_abs_upper|f4}}.
A check on the average would have passed. This one asks for the worst value, so one bad pixel is enough to fail it.

segments.heading: Reproduce before fixing
lines: Before trying any fix, the note on this miss wrote down its predictions, then ran the network on the main processor with the same 16-bit rounding.

The emulation missed by {{primary.emulation.WA.max_abs|f4}}, at the same frame and the same pixel as the chip. So 16-bit arithmetic alone reproduces the miss; no fault in the chip is needed to explain it.

The note had set out two guesses: the weights alone, or the inputs alone. Both were refuted as stated. Rounding only the weights gave {{primary.emulation.W.max_abs|f4}}, and rounding only the inputs gave {{primary.emulation.A.max_abs|f4}}, so either rounding by itself misses the bound.

segments.heading: A sun glint
lines: The bad pixels were single sun glints. At frame 48, one sample on a glossy surface carried {{recipe.noteCase.fireflyRadiance|int}} units of light beside neighbours near {{recipe.noteCase.neighbourRadiance}}.

The denoiser first divides by the surface's specular reflectance, {{recipe.noteCase.specularAlbedo}} plus a small {{recipe.noteCase.eps}}, which turns that sample into about 21,700. Its five by five filter then weighs it down to around a hundred: the note gives 105, against a reference of 110.

segments.heading: The arithmetic
lines: Now the bound. Missing by no more than {{recipe.bound}} on a value of 110 asks for about one part in ten thousand. Near 110, 16-bit marks are {{arithmetic.near110.fp16Spacing}} apart, as we measured last lesson.

The filter itself runs in 32-bit. The rounding happens earlier, in the 16-bit layers that compute the filter's weights. 16-bit numbers hold about one part in a thousand, and any error that size feeding the filter, times a value of 110, moves the answer by about a tenth.

We rebuilt that step at small scale, with a made-up glint of the same size. In our seeded case the stand-in misses by {{recreation.firefly.WA.maxAbs|f4}} with 16-bit inputs and weights, and differs by only {{recreation.firefly.scalar.maxAbs|none}} in 32-bit; across {{sweep.firefly.WA.n|int}} seeds it misses in {{sweep.firefly.WA.over|int}}. Take the glint away and every version passes. These are the stand-in's numbers, not the real network's.

segments.heading: Fixes that fell short
lines: The natural fix is mixed precision: keep the most sensitive layers in 32-bit and the rest on the tensor cores.

In the emulation, with the full-resolution head in 32-bit, the worst difference fell to {{primary.mixed.keep-10.max_abs|f4}}. With three layers, {{primary.mixed.keep-10_1_9.max_abs|f4}}. With six, {{primary.mixed.keep-10_1_9_8_0_3.max_abs|f4}}, on {{primary.mixed.keep-10_1_9_8_0_3.pixels_over_1e-2|int}} pixels. Still over.
None of the mixed splits tried met the bound; 32-bit throughout did.

segments.heading: The bound stays
lines: So the tensor-core path stays unchanged this round, and its parity check still fails. The options named are 32-bit throughout, which costs speed, or a model change that keeps the filter away from values that large, for example filtering a squeezed range and expanding it after, which also affects image quality.
And the note says plainly that the bound is not loosened. In our view that is the lesson: a bound loosened after the miss is seen no longer tests the result. It is fitted to it.

segments.heading: Goodnight
lines: Reproduce the miss, find the arithmetic, and leave the post where you planted it.
Goodnight.
